Senses.PreferredTarget: the step beyond the pole-top, where no footing remains
AlternateTargets: an impossible next step beyond the pole
SearchAliases: step beyond the top of the pole
advance where there is no footing
Senses.Explanation: The step beyond the top of a hundred-foot pole, where the image leaves no footing for another step. The fixed phrase and case title are drawn from Changsha Jingcen's verse: the person sitting atop a hundred-foot pole, although having gained entry, is not yet real; the verse then requires a step forward and says that the worlds in the ten directions are the whole body (百尺竿頭坐底人，雖然得入，未為真；百尺竿頭須進步，十方世界現全身). Wumen Huikai's Case 46 titles the case Stepping Forward from the Pole-top and attributes the question “atop a hundred-foot pole, how does one step forward?” to Shishuang Qingzhu (石霜和尚云，百尺竿頭如何進步). Fojian Huiqin's later verse explicitly names Old Changsha at the time of the pole-top step (百尺竿頭進步時……老長沙). The phrase then circulates as a public question: Yexian Guixing answers “the southern continent, the northern continent” (南贍部洲，北欝單越), Linye Qi answers “then retreat” (退後即得), and Shanduo Zhenzai answers “a beheaded boatman goes down to Yangzhou” (斷頭船子下揚州). Langye Huijue places the pole-top step beside a saying with no intent in the phrase and no phrase in the intent, then asks how to breathe out. Zen bends the impossible ordinary action into a named case, a quoted verse-line, and a repeatedly answered public question; the records give different answers without changing the action denoted.
Senses.Note: The headword has 113 hits in 81 allowlisted texts. Six exact witnesses plus one marked family verse cover case title, Changsha attribution, early lamp discourse, public interviews, and later commentary. Title, quotation, instruction, and question all name the same step from the same pole-top image, not different things.

Occurrences.Kwic: 竿頭進步石霜和尚云。百尺竿頭如何進步。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen's Barrier (無門關), Case 46 compiled by Wumen Huikai, gives the case title and explicitly attributes the headword-bearing pole-top question to Shishuang Qingzhu; Wumen is the compiler and case commentator.

Occurrences.Kwic: 百尺竿頭坐底人。雖然得入。未為真。百尺竿頭須進步十方世界現全身。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wumen's Barrier (無門關) preserves the old verse without naming its speaker there; the parallel Linked Pearl Collection places the exchange in Changsha Jingcen's section and explicitly introduces it as the master's displayed verse. The exact joined headword is absent, so this remains family evidence.

Occurrences.Kwic: 百尺竿頭進步時築着磕著自家底老長沙
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Linked Pearl Collection of Chan Eulogies on Ancient Cases (禪宗頌古聯珠通集) attributes this verse to Fojian Huiqin, who explicitly names Old Changsha at the time of the pole-top step.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問如何是百尺竿頭進步底句師云南贍部洲北欝單越
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Old Recorded Sayings of Venerable Masters (古尊宿語錄), in Yexian Guixing's record, preserves an unnamed monk speaking the exact public pole-top-step question; Yexian answers with the southern and northern continents without repeating the headword. All six attribution rungs leave the monk personally unnamed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧參，問：「百尺竿頭進步時如何？」師云：「退後即得。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Recorded Sayings of Linye Qi (林野奇禪師語錄), an unnamed visiting monk speaks the exact pole-top-step question; Linye answers, ‘then retreat,’ without repeating the headword. All six attribution rungs leave the monk personally unnamed.

Occurrences.Kwic: 猷蒙指示，竿頭進步事如何？」師曰：「斷頭船子下揚州。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In the Recorded Sayings of Shanduo Zhenzai (山鐸真在禪師語錄), the expanded exchange explicitly names Gulun (古輪) as the monk who speaks the exact pole-top-step question; Shanduo answers with a beheaded boatman going down to Yangzhou without repeating the headword. Occurrences.Kwic: 若能如是，方解百尺竿頭進步，句中無意，意中無句。既然如是，且作麼生吐氣？
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Joint Essentials of the Lamps (聯燈會要), section on Langye Huijue, records Langye joining the pole-top step to phrase and intent and then asking how to breathe out.
